subtitleEn: The Rock whose food we have eaten
heTitleNote: Friday night, after the meal and before Birkat HaMazon
progression: | Am Am | Dm Am | E E | Am Am |
metaLine: 92 BPM · 4/4 · sung at the end of the Friday night meal, immediately before the grace after meals · four stanzas, each answered by the same refrain
intro: The zemer that ends the Friday night meal, sung immediately before the grace after meals — and in fact it is a compressed version of that grace, saying the same four things in four stanzas. Everyone at the table knows the refrain, which returns after each stanza and is the same nine words every time. That is not laziness: the refrain is what lets a table of people who do not read Hebrew sing along for five minutes, and it is why this is the first zemer most guests learn.

stanzas.label: refrain

lines.en: The Rock, of whose food we have eaten — bless Him, my faithful ones!
We are satisfied and we have food to spare, as the LORD said.

stanzas.summary: Two lines that will come back four times. {{0.1}} literally means "of that which is His": what was eaten was never the host's. And {{1.1}} — leaving food over — is not politeness but a quotation, from the story of Elisha and the twenty loaves in Kings, where the miracle is the leftovers.

stanzas.label: who feeds

lines.en: He feeds His world, our Shepherd, our Father;
we have eaten His bread and drunk His wine.
Therefore we give thanks to His name and praise Him with our mouths,
saying and answering: there is none holy like the LORD.
The Rock, of whose food we have eaten — bless Him, my faithful ones! We are satisfied and we have food to spare, as the LORD said.

stanzas.summary: The first of the four blessings of the grace after meals, in four lines: the one who feeds. {{2.3}} and {{2.4}} sit side by side — shepherd and father — and the poem does not choose between them. {{5.4}} is a phrase from Hannah's prayer in Samuel, dropped in without introduction, which is how these poems work.

stanzas.label: for the land

lines.en: With song and the sound of thanksgiving we will bless our God,
for a desirable land, a good one, that He gave our ancestors to inherit;
food and provision He has given our soul its fill,
His kindness has prevailed over us, and the LORD's truth.
The Rock, of whose food we have eaten — bless Him, my faithful ones! We are satisfied and we have food to spare, as the LORD said.

stanzas.summary: The second blessing: for the land. {{10.0}} and {{10.3}} are the pair that runs through the psalms, kindness and truth, and the last line is Psalm 117 almost word for word — the shortest psalm in the book, folded into a table song.

stanzas.label: for Jerusalem

lines.en: Have mercy in Your kindness on Your people, our Rock,
on Zion, the dwelling of Your glory, the abode of our house of splendour;
may the son of David Your servant come and redeem us,
the breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the LORD.
The Rock, of whose food we have eaten — bless Him, my faithful ones! We are satisfied and we have food to spare, as the LORD said.

stanzas.summary: The third blessing: for Jerusalem. {{15.0}} and {{15.1}} — the breath of our nostrils — is from Lamentations, where it describes the captured king, and here it is turned toward a king not yet come. A phrase written in defeat, reused as a hope.

stanzas.label: the Temple

lines.en: May the Temple be rebuilt, may the city of Zion be filled,
and there we will sing a new song, and go up with rejoicing;
may the Merciful One, the Holy One, be blessed and exalted,
over a full cup of wine, according to the blessing of the LORD.
The Rock, of whose food we have eaten — bless Him, my faithful ones! We are satisfied and we have food to spare, as the LORD said.

stanzas.summary: The last stanza brings the poem back to the table it is being sung at: {{20.1}}, {{20.2}}, {{20.3}} — a full cup of wine, which is the cup of the grace after meals, sitting in front of whoever is leading. The poem ends by pointing at the object in the room.

chantTips: The refrain is everything. If you learn nine words of this song, learn {{0.0}} through {{1.3}}, and you can join any Friday night table in the country.
The verses are usually taken by one or two people who know them; the whole table comes in on the refrain. Leave a clear breath before it so people know it is coming.
Around 92 BPM, and it does not accelerate. This one is sung sitting down, at the end of a long meal.
Three chords carry it. Am for the openings, Dm and E for the turns, back to Am for every refrain.

about.h: It is the grace after meals in miniature
about.body: The four stanzas match the four blessings of Birkat HaMazon in order: the one who feeds, the land, Jerusalem, and the closing blessing. It is sung immediately before the real thing, which makes it a rehearsal and a summary at once.

The poem carries no acrostic naming its author and no attribution in the manuscripts, which is unusual for a zemer of this period — Dror Yikra names Dunash, Yah Ribon names Najara. This one arrived without a signature and is generally dated to the fourteenth century or thereabouts.

Almost every line closes on a phrase from the Tanakh, and the phrases are not marked as quotations. Elisha's leftovers, Hannah's prayer, Psalm 117, Lamentations. A listener who knows the sources hears a second poem underneath the first, and a listener who does not still gets a complete one.
